original_question.stem:
Consider the following facts: After forty years of planned development, India achieved a strong industrial base and became self-sufficient in the production of food grains. In 1991, a crisis in the balance of payments led to the introduction of economic reforms.

Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Forty years of planned development
(B) Strong industrial base
(C) Self-sufficiency in the production of food grains
(D) 1991 balance-of-payments crisis

List-II
(I) Led to the introduction of economic reforms
(II) Achievement stated for India after planned development
(III) Achievement in food-grain production stated for India
(IV) Period after which the two achievements in (II) and (III) are reported

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
B. (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
C. (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
D. (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)

items.original_explanation: The stem states that the strong industrial base and self-sufficiency in food-grain production were achievements after forty years of planned development. It separately states that the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis led to the introduction of reforms. Therefore, the complete matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III) and (D)-(I).

reasons: The stem states that forty years of planned development preceded both achievements: a strong industrial base and self-sufficiency in food grains. Thus A-IV, B-II and C-III.
It also states that the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis led to economic reforms, so D-I. These pairings appear together only in option C.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Background to the 1991 reforms: achievements after planned development and the balance-of-payments crisis.

answer_conditions.condition: Forty years of planned development is the period preceding the two stated achievements.
A strong industrial base is an achievement stated after planned development.
Self-sufficiency in food-grain production is the food-grain achievement stated after planned development.
The 1991 balance-of-payments crisis led to the introduction of economic reforms.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: If II and III were transposed, A's achievement pairings would fit; the printed list instead makes III food-grain-specific and II the broader post-planning achievement.
If II described a period and IV an achievement, B's first two pairings could fit; the printed descriptions assign those roles oppositely.
If I described the food-grain achievement and III the cause of reforms, D's last two pairings could fit; the stem states the reverse.

original_question.stem:
Arrange the following steps in the correct sequence for constructing a market supply curve from the supply schedules of the same firms at a range of market prices.
(A) Add the quantities supplied by all firms at a given market price.
(B) Read the quantity supplied by each firm at that market price.
(C) Repeat the process for other market prices.
(D) Plot the aggregate quantity supplied against the corresponding market price.

items.original_explanation: At a given market price, first read each firm's quantity supplied and then add these quantities to find market supply at that price. Repeat this for other prices, then plot aggregate quantities against the corresponding prices to obtain the market supply curve.

reasons: The intended procedure is to read each firm's quantity at a given price, sum those quantities, repeat across prices, and plot the aggregate quantities against price: option B.
Option C can also work if the firm quantities are read for all prices first and then summed price by price. The stem does not specify that summing must happen before moving to other prices.

Defect: multiple_correct_options: Option C is defensible if firm quantities are gathered at each price before the totals are calculated price by price. The stem does not require summing at one price before repeating the reading step for other prices.

Defect: missing_decisive_assumption: option C is correct if Read every firm's quantity at each price first, repeat that data-gathering across prices, then sum quantities within each price and plot the totals.
Condition implied_decisive: The steps imply completing the reading and summation at one price before repeating the entire operation at other prices.

supporting_excerpts.text: 67 under Perfect Competition The Theory of the Firm • In a perfectly competitive market, firms are price-takers. • The total revenue of a firm is the market price of the good multiplied by the firm’s output of the good. • For a price-taking firm, average revenue is equal to market price. • For a price-taking firm, marginal revenue is equal to market price. • The demand curve that a firm faces in a perfectly competitive market is perfectly elastic; it is a horizontal straight line at the market price. • The profit of a firm is the difference between total revenue earned and total cost incurred. • If there is a positive level of output at which a firm’s profit is maximised in the short run, three conditions must hold at that output level (i) p = SMC (ii) SMC is non-decreasing (iii) p ≥ AV C. • If there is a positive level of output at which a firm’s profit is maximised in the long run, three conditions must hold at that output level (i) p = LRMC (ii) LRMC is non-decreasing (iii) p ≥ LRAC. • The short run supply curve of a firm is the rising part of the SMC curve from and above minimum AVC together with 0 output for all prices less than the minimum AVC. • The long run supply curve of a firm is the rising part of the LRMC curve from and above minimum LRAC together with 0 output for all prices less than the minimum LRAC. • Technological progress is expected to shift the supply curve of a firm to the right. • An increase (decrease) in input prices is expected to shift the supply curve of a firm to the left (right). • The imposition of a unit tax shifts the supply curve of a firm to the left. • The market supply curve is obtained by the horizontal summation of the supply curves of individual firms. • The price elasticity of supply of a good is the percentage change in quantity supplied due to one per cent change in the market price of the good. ssssseeeeesssssiiiiicccccrrrrreeeeexxxxxEEEEE yyyyyrrrrraaaaammmmmmmmmmuuuuuSSSSS 1. original_question.stem: A planning review summarises two findings for India after forty years of planned development: (i) a strong industrial base had been achieved and food-grain production had become self-sufficient; (ii) a major segment of the population continued to depend on agriculture for its livelihood. Treat both findings as accurate. A reviewer argues that finding (ii) cannot be true once finding (i) is true. Which assessment best applies the findings?
options: The reviewer is correct: food-grain self-sufficiency rules out continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.
The reviewer is correct: a strong industrial base rules out continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.
The reviewer is incorrect: food-grain self-sufficiency can coexist with continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.
The reviewer is incorrect: the food-grain achievement shows that the major segment dependent on agriculture had shifted to industrial livelihoods.

items.original_explanation: The findings concern food-grain production and livelihood dependence, respectively. The stated excerpt reports both outcomes together, so food-grain self-sufficiency does not rule out continued dependence on agriculture for livelihood.

reasons: C is correct: the stem stipulates that both findings are accurate, and E1.1 explicitly reports food-grain self-sufficiency alongside continued agricultural livelihood dependence. Those outcomes are compatible.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Achievements and continuing challenges of planned development, including food-grain self-sufficiency and dependence on agriculture for livelihoods.

answer_conditions.condition: Food-grain production is self-sufficient, as stated in finding (i).
A major segment of the population continues to depend on agriculture for its livelihood, as stated in finding (ii).
Both findings are to be treated as accurate together.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: One might infer that food-grain self-sufficiency means agriculture no longer supports many livelihoods, but finding (ii) explicitly says otherwise.
One might read a strong industrial base as replacing agricultural livelihoods, but the stem explicitly retains substantial agricultural dependence.
If industrial growth had absorbed the agricultural workforce, livelihoods could have shifted; the stem instead says a major segment still depends on agriculture.

style_notes: The stem stipulates both propositions and C restates their compatibility, so the answer can be found by checking consistency without economics knowledge.

level_calibration.evidence: The stem itself supplies both claims as accurate; resolving their compatibility requires no subject knowledge.

discrimination_value.evidence: The key directly restates the compatibility of the two stipulated findings.

original_question.stem: During a budget period, a government records only these receipts: revenue receipts of ₹2,40,000, fresh loans of ₹1,20,000, and ₹35,000 from selling shares in a public sector undertaking. What is the total amount of capital receipts for the period?

items.original_explanation: A fresh loan creates a liability, and selling government shares reduces the government’s financial assets; both are capital receipts. Therefore, total capital receipts are ₹1,20,000 + ₹35,000 = ₹1,55,000, excluding the stated revenue receipts.

reasons: Fresh loans are capital receipts because they create liabilities; proceeds from selling government PSU shares are capital receipts because they reduce financial assets.
Exclude the ₹2,40,000 in revenue receipts. Add the two capital receipts: ₹1,20,000 + ₹35,000 = ₹1,55,000.

original_question.stem:
Consider the following statements about the paradox of thrift. It states that if all people increase the proportion of income they save, total savings will not increase; they will either decline or remain unchanged. In an illustration, aggregate saving is 10 both before and after an increase in thrift.
(A) An increase in the proportion of income saved necessarily raises total savings.
(B) When people become more thrifty, total savings may remain unchanged.
(C) Total savings must decline whenever people become more thrifty.
(D) In the illustration, aggregate saving is 10 at both points.
Choose the correct answer using the options below:

items.original_explanation: The paradox of thrift states that total savings do not increase when people raise the proportion of income they save; savings may remain unchanged. In the illustration, aggregate saving is 10 both before and after the increase in thrift. Therefore, statements (B) and (D) are correct.

reasons: The stated paradox allows aggregate saving to decline or remain unchanged, so (A) and (C) are false while (B) is true. The illustration explicitly gives saving as 10 at both points, making (D) true; the matching answer is D.
The rule and equal-saving example are supported by E1.1 and E1.5.

answer_conditions.condition: The paradox is applied to an increase in the proportion of income saved by all people.

The illustration states aggregate saving is 10 before and after the increase in thrift.

A's necessary increase conflicts with C's necessary decline; moreover, D is explicitly true, so this cannot be the complete correct set.
Only by disregarding the stated unchanged aggregate saving could C's universal decline claim hold; D itself is explicitly true.

original_question.stem:
An economy records the following changes:
Year 1 to Year 2: GDP index rises from 200 to 220; employed persons increase from 80 million to 84 million.
Year 2 to Year 3: GDP index rises from 220 to 242; employed persons remain at 84 million.
Calculate percentage changes using (final value − initial value) ÷ initial value × 100. For this question, an increase in the GDP index represents an increase in production of goods and services, and jobless growth means an increase in production without generating employment. Which statement is correct?
options: GDP grew by 10% in each interval; employment grew by 5% and then 0%, so Year 2 to Year 3 shows jobless growth.
GDP grew by 10% in each interval; employment grew by 5% in each interval, so neither interval shows jobless growth.
GDP grew by 10% in each interval; employment grew by 5% and then 0%, so Year 1 to Year 2 shows jobless growth.
GDP grew by 10% and 9.09% in the two intervals; employment grew by 5% and then 0%, so Year 2 to Year 3 shows jobless growth.

items.original_explanation: From Year 1 to Year 2, GDP growth is (220 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 10%, and employment growth is (84 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = 5%. From Year 2 to Year 3, GDP growth is (242 − 220) ÷ 220 × 100 = 10%, while employment growth is 0%. Thus, production increases without generating employment in the second interval, which meets the stated meaning of jobless growth.

reasons: Given the stem's definition, production rises without generating employment in Year 2 to Year 3 only. E1.1 supports the jobless-growth concept.

original_question.stem:
A review considers four issues in organic farming. Match each issue in List-I with the corresponding implication in List-II.

List-I
(A) Comparing organic yields with yields from modern agricultural farming during the initial years
(B) A small or marginal farmer considering adaptation to large-scale organic production
(C) Comparing organic produce with sprayed produce for blemishes and shelf life
(D) Planning the range of off-season crops under organic farming

List-II
(I) The choice of off-season crops is quite limited.
(II) Organic produce may have more blemishes and a shorter shelf life.
(III) Organic yields are lower during the initial years than yields from modern agricultural farming.
(IV) Small and marginal farmers may find adaptation to large-scale production difficult.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

A. (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
B. (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
C. (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
D. (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)

original_question.stem: An account cites villagers’ use of e-mail as an example of transformation, projects e-governance as a way of the future, and states that the value of IT depends greatly on the existing level of economic development. It raises, without answering, whether IT-based services in rural areas lead to human development. An agency compares two rural areas with different existing levels of economic development. Which conclusion is supported by the stated principle?
options: The value of IT should be assessed in relation to each area’s existing level of economic development.
Villagers’ use of e-mail establishes that IT has equal value across the two areas.
The projection of e-governance establishes that IT’s value is independent of economic development.
The discussion question establishes that rural IT services lead to human development.

items.original_explanation: The stated relationship makes each area’s existing level of economic development relevant when assessing the value of IT. The e-mail example, the projection of e-governance and the open discussion question do not establish the conclusions in options B, C and D.

original_question.stem:
For one period, an economy has GVA at factor cost of ₹8,00,000. It pays production taxes of ₹70,000 and product taxes of ₹50,000, and receives production subsidies of ₹10,000 and product subsidies of ₹20,000. These are the only production taxes, product taxes and subsidies for the period.

Consider the following statements:
(A) Net production taxes are ₹60,000.
(B) GVA at basic prices is ₹8,60,000.
(C) Net product taxes are ₹30,000.
(D) GDP at market prices is ₹8,80,000.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

items.original_explanation: Net production taxes are ₹70,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹60,000, so GVA at basic prices is ₹8,00,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹8,60,000. Net product taxes are ₹50,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹30,000, so GDP at market prices is ₹8,60,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹8,90,000. Thus statements (A), (B) and (C) are correct, while (D) is not.

supporting_excerpts.text: 24 2424 2424Introductory Macroeconomics 4 In this example, we have left out factor payments in the form of rent and interest. But this will not make any difference to the basic result, because after paying wages the remainder of value added by a firm will be distributed between rent, interest and profits (together called operating surplus). Table 2.3: Distributions of factor incomes of firms A and B Firm A Firm B Wages 20 60 Profits 30 90 Recall that GDP by income method = sum total of factor incomes, which is equal to total wages received (workers of A and B) and total profits earned (by A and B), which is equal4 to 80 + 120 = 200. 2.2.4 Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices In India, the most highlighted measure of national income has been the GDP at factor cost. The Central Statistics Office (CSO) of the Government of India has been reporting the GDP at factor cost and at market prices. In its revision in January 2015 the CSO replaced GDP at factor cost with the GVA at basic prices, and the GDP at market prices, which is now called only GDP, is now the most highlighted measure. The idea of GVA has already been discussed: it is the value of total output produced in the economy less the value of intermediate consumption (the output which is used in production of output further, and not used in final consumption). Here we discuss the concept of basic prices. The distinction between factor cost, basic prices and market prices is based on the distinction between net production taxes (production taxes less production subsidies) and net product taxes (product taxes less product subsidies). Production taxes and subsidies are paid or received in relation to production and are independent of the volume of production such as land revenues, stamp and registration fee. Product taxes and subsidies, on the other hand, are paid or received per unit or product, e.g., excise tax, service tax, export and import duties etc. Factor cost includes only the payment to factors of production, it does not include any tax. In order to arrive at the market prices, we have to add to the factor cost the total indirect taxes less total subsidies. The basic prices lie in between: they include the production taxes (less production subsidies) but not product taxes (less product subsidies). Therefore in order to arrive at market prices we have to add product taxes (less product subsidies) to the basic prices. As stated above, now the CSO releases GVA at basic prices. Thus, it includes the net production taxes but not net product taxes. In order to arrive at the GDP (at market prices) we need to add net pr oduct taxes to GV A at basic prices. Thus, GVA at factor costs + Net production taxes = GVA at basic prices GVA at basic prices + Net product taxes = GVA at market prices Table 2.5 at the end of the chapter gives the figures for GDP (at market prices) and GVA at basic prices, while T able 2.6 gives the composition of GDP fr om expenditure side. The ratio of nominal to real GDP is a well known index of prices. This is called GDP Deflator.

original_question.stem:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Varying degrees and types of land degradation stem mainly from unstable and inappropriate use.
(B) In urban cities, vehicular pollution is given special reference within a major environmental concern.
(C) Management of fresh water is identified as a priority issue.

(I) Air pollution

items.original_explanation: Unstable and inappropriate use is linked to land degradation, while vehicular pollution in urban cities is specified as a special reference within air pollution. The identified priorities of management of fresh water and solid waste match their corresponding categories. Thus, option A gives all four correct pairings.

It identifies air pollution with special reference to vehicular pollution in urban cities, so (B) matches (I). Its priority-issues list also directly matches fresh-water management to (III) and solid-waste management to (II).

original_question.stem:
A producer plans to add ₹1,20,000 to inventory by the end of the year. To meet extra demand, she later sells goods worth ₹35,000 from that inventory. Assume no other changes to inventory occur. Arrange the following events and steps in the order that leads from the producer’s plan to identifying actual investment.
(A) The producer plans an addition of ₹1,20,000 to inventory.
(B) The producer sells ₹35,000 worth of goods from inventory to meet extra demand.
(C) The net increase in inventory is calculated as ₹1,20,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹85,000.
(D) The amount of ₹85,000 is identified as actual (ex post) investment.
Choose the correct sequence:
A. (A)-(C)-(B)-(D)
B. (B)-(A)-(C)-(D)
C. (A)-(B)-(C)-(D)
D. (A)-(B)-(D)-(C)

items.original_explanation: The planned addition is ₹1,20,000, and the later sale from inventory reduces the net increase by ₹35,000. Thus, actual investment is ₹1,20,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹85,000. The plan and sale must be accounted for before calculating and identifying the actual investment.

reasons: The plan is stated to precede the later sale, so A comes before B.

The sale reduces the planned inventory addition: ₹1,20,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹85,000. With no other inventory changes, this is the actual increase in inventory, identified as actual (ex-post) investment after the calculation.
Thus the order is A-B-C-D, option C. The supplied excerpt supports the planned-versus-actual inventory-investment distinction and the meaning of ex-ante and ex-post.

original_question.stem: A review of India reports that the population share working in agriculture was 67.5% in 1950 and 64.9% in 1990. Industry’s share of GDP was 13% in 1950–51 and 24.6% in 1990–91, and the industrial sector’s annual growth rate during the period was 6%. The review also reports that industry and services did not absorb the people working in agriculture. A commentator concludes that the rise in industry’s GDP share demonstrates a comparable transfer of workers from agriculture to industry. Which assessment follows from the stated facts?
options: The conclusion follows because the 11.6-percentage-point rise in industry’s GDP share measures an equivalent movement of workers out of agriculture.

The conclusion does not follow: industry’s GDP share rose by 11.6 percentage points, while agriculture’s population share fell by 2.6 percentage points, and industry and services did not absorb the agricultural workforce.
The conclusion follows because a 6% annual industrial growth rate establishes that industry absorbed the workers corresponding to agriculture’s 2.6-percentage-point decline.
The conclusion does not follow because agriculture’s population share increased by 2.6 percentage points, offsetting the increase in industry’s GDP share.

items.original_explanation: Industry’s GDP share increased by 24.6 − 13 = 11.6 percentage points, whereas the population share working in agriculture decreased by 67.5 − 64.9 = 2.6 percentage points. These are different measures, and the case states that industry and services did not absorb the agricultural workforce. Therefore, the increase in industry’s GDP share, even alongside the stated growth rate, does not demonstrate a comparable transfer of workers to industry.

reasons: Industry’s GDP share rose by 24.6 − 13 = 11.6 percentage points. Agriculture’s population share fell by 67.5 − 64.9 = 2.6 percentage points.
The reported GDP-share rise does not establish a comparable worker transfer; the stated fact that industry and services did not absorb the agricultural workforce directly contradicts that inference.
The 6% annual industrial growth rate does not overturn the stated non-absorption fact, and option D reverses the direction of agriculture’s change.

Arrange the statements in the logical order of the concluding argument, with the government response at the end.
(A) The structure of the workforce in India has changed.
(B) Newly emerging jobs are found mostly in the service sector.

original_question.stem: A catalogue entry describes a textile as cotton muslin from Bengal and records a foreign traveller’s label, “malmal khas”. No surviving record identifies who wore this particular textile. What does the label imply?
options: It indicates that the textile is silk rather than cotton.
It indicates that the muslin is an ordinary variety rather than the finest variety.
It indicates that a particular royal person actually wore this textile.
It indicates that the textile was worn by, or fit for, royalty.

items.original_explanation: Malmal was the finest variety of muslin, and “malmal khas” implied that it was worn by, or fit for, royalty. The label expresses a royal association; it does not establish that a particular royal person actually wore this textile.

supporting_excerpts.text: 4 INDIAN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 1.1 I NTRODUCTION The primary objective of this book, Indian Economic Development , is to familiarise you with the basic features of the Indian economy, and its development, as it is today, in the aftermath of Independence. However, it is equally important to know something about the country’s economic past even as you learn about its present state and future prospects. So, let us first look at the state of India’s economy prior to the country’s independence and form an idea of the various considerations that shaped India’ s post-independence development strategy. The structure of India’s present- day economy is not just of current making; it has its roots steeped in history, particularly in the period when India was under British rule which lasted for almost two centuries before India finally won its independence on 15 August 1947. The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain’s own rapidly expanding modern industrial base. An understanding of the exploitative nature of this relationship is essential for any assessment of the kind and level of development which the Indian economy has been able to attain over the last seven and half decades. 1.2 1.2 LOW LEVEL OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT UNDER THE COLONIAL RULE India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities. India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc. These products enjoyed a worldwide market based on the reputation of the fine quality of material used and the high standards of craftsmanship seen in all imports from India (See Box 1.1). “India is the pivot of our Empire... If the Empire loses any other part of its Dominion we can survive, but if we lose India, the sun of our Empire will have set.” Victor Alexander Vruce, the Viceroy of British India in 1894 Box 1.1: Textile Industry in Bengal Muslin is a type of cotton textile which had its origin in Bengal, particularly, places in and around Dhaka (spelled during the pre-independence period as Dacca), now the capital city of Bangladesh. ‘Daccai Muslin’ had gained worldwide fame as an exquisite type of cotton textile. The finest variety of muslin was called malmal. Sometimes, foreign travellers also used to refer to it as malmal shahi or malmal khas implying that it was wor n by, or fit for , the royalty. Reprint 2026-27

The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.

original_question.stem: A research team wants to investigate the economy as a whole, rather than the behaviour of an individual consumer or producer or the price and quantity in a single-commodity market. Which research question best fits this aim?
options: How are price and quantity determined in the market for one commodity?
How does an individual consumer behave in relation to one commodity?
How does total output in the economy grow over time?
How does an individual producer behave in producing one commodity?

items.original_explanation: The question about how total output in the economy grows over time concerns an aggregate measure and its change over time, so it is macroeconomic. The other questions concern a single-commodity market or an individual consumer or producer, which are microeconomic topics.

reasons: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole using aggregate measures, including total output, and asks how total output grows over time. That directly matches option C.
Options A, B and D concern a single-commodity market or an individual consumer or producer, which the stem distinguishes from its economy-wide aim.

original_question.stem: For one financial year, a government has a fiscal deficit of ₹8,40,000. Its interest payments are ₹1,20,000, and its interest receipts on net domestic lending are ₹20,000. Assume these are the only interest payments and receipts relevant to the calculation. What is the government’s primary deficit?

items.original_explanation: Net interest liabilities = ₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,00,000. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − net interest liabilities = ₹8,40,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹7,40,000, so option C is correct.

reasons: The supplied definition gives primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments: ₹8,40,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹7,20,000 (A).

The excerpt separately describes gross primary deficit using net interest liabilities; subtracting the ₹1,00,000 net interest liabilities gives ₹7,40,000, but that is not the measure named in the question.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Government budget: measures of government deficit, including primary deficit

answer_conditions.condition: The requested measure is primary deficit, rather than gross primary deficit.
Fiscal deficit is ₹8,40,000 for the stated financial year.
Interest payments are ₹1,20,000 for that financial year.
Interest receipts on net domestic lending are ₹20,000.
No other relevant interest payments or receipts are to be included.
For primary deficit, subtract interest payments from fiscal deficit; the excerpt distinguishes this from gross primary deficit calculated using net interest liabilities.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: Add net interest liabilities to the fiscal deficit: ₹8,40,000 + (₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000) = ₹9,40,000.
Interpret the requested measure as gross primary deficit and subtract net interest liabilities: ₹8,40,000 − (₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000) = ₹7,40,000.
Subtract only the interest receipt from fiscal deficit: ₹8,40,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹8,20,000.

style_notes: The interest-receipt figure is extraneous to the stated primary-deficit calculation and may cue the separate gross-primary-deficit measure.

original_question.stem:
Use the following unemployment data for the same youth snapshot (2011–12): male youth with graduation and above had rates of 19 per cent in rural areas and 16 per cent in urban areas; young rural female graduates had a rate of nearly 30 per cent; male youth with primary-level education in rural and urban areas had a rate of about 3–6 per cent. List-I

(B) Difference between rates for rural female and rural male graduates
(C) Group with the highest reported unemployment rate among those listed
(D) Male youth with primary-level education in rural and urban areas compared with male youth with graduation and above
List-II
(I) Rural male graduates: 3 percentage points higher than urban male graduates
(II) Rural female graduates: nearly 11 percentage points higher than rural male graduates

supporting_excerpts.text: 5INDIAN ECONOMY ON THE EVE OF INDEPENDENCE The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain. Obviously, the colonial govern - ment never made any sincere attempt to estimate India’s national and per capita income . Some individual attempts which were made to measure such incomes yielded conflicting and inconsistent results. Among the notable estimators — Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V .K.R.V . Rao and R.C. Desai — it was Rao , whose estimates during the colonial period was considered very significant. However , most studies did find that the country’s growth of aggregate real output during the first half of the twentieth century was less than two per cent coupled with a meagre half per cent growth in per capita output per year. 1.3 A GRICULTURAL S ECTOR India’s economy under the British colonial rule remained fundamentally agrarian — about 85 per cent of the country’s population lived mostly in villages and derived livelihood directly or indirectly from agriculture (See Box 1.2). metadata.topic: Production & Costs: focus on this supplied section: 49 Production and Costs Just like the short run, in the long run, the sum of all marginal costs up to some output level gives us the total cost at that level. Shapes of the Long Ru. Test a distinct implication, application or calculation supported by it.

original_question.stem:
A firm records the following three successive long-run production transitions. In each transition, all inputs increase by the same proportion. Input prices remain unchanged, and each listed cost is the cost of the input bundle used for that output.
Interval I: Output rises from 80 to 120 units; input-bundle cost rises from ₹2,00,000 to ₹2,80,000.
Interval II: Output rises from 120 to 180 units; input-bundle cost rises from ₹2,80,000 to ₹4,20,000.
Interval III: Output rises from 180 to 270 units; input-bundle cost rises from ₹4,20,000 to ₹6,51,000.
Which option correctly classifies the returns to scale in Intervals I, II and III, respectively?
options: Interval I: CRS; Interval II: IRS; Interval III: DRS.
Interval I: IRS; Interval II: CRS; Interval III: DRS.
Interval I: DRS; Interval II: CRS; Interval III: IRS.
Interval I: IRS; Interval II: DRS; Interval III: CRS.

items.original_explanation: Output rises by 50% in each interval. With unchanged input prices and all inputs scaled by the same proportion, the input-bundle cost changes by the same proportion as the inputs. In Interval I, cost rises by 40%, less than output, so IRS operates; in Interval II, both rise by 50%, so CRS operates; in Interval III, cost rises by 55%, more than output, so DRS operates.

reasons: Output rises by a factor of 1.5 in each interval. Input prices are unchanged, so each input-bundle cost factor indicates the input-scale factor.
Interval I: cost factor 2.80/2.00 = 1.40, less than 1.5, so output rises proportionally more than inputs: IRS.

original_question.stem: A district assessment uses comparable index values for demand for environmental resources and services and their available supply. Define the gap as the demand index minus the supply index. In an earlier assessment, demand was 70 and supply was 100; in a later assessment, demand was 130 and supply was 100. The assessment attributes the limited supply to overuse. Which option correctly calculates the movement in the gap and interprets it?
options: The earlier gap is +30 and the later gap is −30, a 60-point movement towards excess supply.
The earlier gap is −30 and the later gap is +30, a 60-point movement towards excess demand.
The earlier gap is −30 and the later gap is +30, a 30-point increase in the gap.
The earlier gap is −30 and the later gap is −30, so the relationship is unchanged.

items.original_explanation: The earlier gap is 70 − 100 = −30, while the later gap is 130 − 100 = +30. The change is +30 − (−30) = 60 index points, moving from supply exceeding demand to demand exceeding supply. This is a reversal of the supply-demand relationship, with the stated limited supply attributed to overuse.

reasons: Using the stated definition, the earlier gap is 70 − 100 = −30 and the later gap is 130 − 100 = +30.

The gap therefore increases by 30 − (−30) = 60 points. The positive later gap means demand exceeds supply; the NCERT excerpt describes increased demand alongside supply limited by overuse (E1.2, E2.1).

However, it is equally important to know something about the country’s economic past even as you learn about its present state and future prospects. So, let us first look at the state of India’s economy prior to the country’s independence and form an idea of the various considerations that shaped India’ s post-independence development strategy. The structure of India’s present- day economy is not just of current making; it has its roots steeped in history, particularly in the period when India was under British rule which lasted for almost two centuries before India finally won its independence on 15 August 1947. The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain’s own rapidly expanding modern industrial base. An understanding of the exploitative nature of this relationship is essential for any assessment of the kind and level of development which the Indian economy has been able to attain over the last seven and half decades. 1.2 1.2 LOW LEVEL OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT UNDER THE COLONIAL RULE India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. original_question.stem: Two cases operate under the same final-goods multiplier model. Assume each case starts from equilibrium, the stated autonomous-expenditure increment is the only initial change in aggregate demand, and the mpc remains constant throughout the adjustment. In Case II, the autonomous-expenditure increment is ₹18 lakh, and the mpc is higher than in Case I by 0.05 (five percentage points). In each case, the investment multiplier is 1/(1 − c), where c is the mpc, and the total output increment equals the multiplier multiplied by the autonomous-expenditure increment. What is the total equilibrium output increment in Case II?

items.original_explanation: In Case I, the multiplier is ₹84 lakh ÷ ₹21 lakh = 4, so c = 0.75. In Case II, c = 0.80, making the multiplier 1/(1 − 0.80) = 5; therefore, the total output increment is 5 × ₹18 lakh = ₹90 lakh.

These terms, however, can be used with a different connotation. Consumption may denote not what people have actually consumed in a given year, but what they Reprint 2026-27
54 5454 5454Introductory Macroeconomics had planned to consume during the same period. Similarly, investment can mean the amount a producer plans to add to her inventory. It may be different from what she ends up doing. Suppose the producer plans to add Rs 100 worth goods to her stock by the end of the year. Her planned investment is, therefore, Rs 100 in that year. However, due to an unforeseen upsurge of demand for her goods in the market the volume of her sales exceeds what she had planned to sell and, to meet this extra demand, she has to sell goods worth Rs 30 from her stock. Therefore, at the end of the year , her inventory goes up by Rs (100 – 30) = Rs 70 only. Her planned investment is Rs 100 whereas her actual, or ex post, investment is Rs 70 only. We call the planned values of the variables – consumption, investment or output of final goods – their ex ante measures.

original_question.stem: A groundwater resource is replenished at a constant rate of 32 lakh litres per month. Over a three-month period, existing users will withdraw 43 lakh litres in total. A proposed project requests a further 58 lakh litres during the same period; these are the only withdrawals. For this calculation, apply only the condition that total resource extraction over the period must not exceed regeneration over that period. original_question.stem: A village committee reviews a proposed paper mill that would use forest materials as industrial raw material. The mill is projected to employ 600 workers, and 1,200 residents use the same forest to meet daily needs. The government has allocated the forestland, but the proposal does not assess whether industrial use would restrict residents’ access; employment is its only quantified benefit. The industrialist argues that the job estimate and the allocation establish that the proposal is acceptable. Which response is best supported?
options: Reject the proposal solely because it involves industrial use of forest materials.
Assess whether residents’ daily needs would be deprived and weigh that impact alongside the employment offered.
Approve the proposal because its projected jobs establish that its benefits exceed its costs.
Treat the forestland allocation as evidence that residents’ daily needs are protected.

items.original_explanation: The stated comparison makes the effect on people’s daily needs relevant when considering the employment offered by industrial use of forest materials. The proposal does not establish whether residents’ access would be restricted, so that impact must be assessed rather than treating the job estimate or land allocation as decisive.

reasons: The supplied textbook excerpt presents the same paper-mill trade-off and questions whether employment makes industrial use acceptable when residents’ daily needs may be deprived.

Because the proposal has not assessed whether access would be restricted, B is the supported response: assess that effect and consider it alongside employment, rather than assuming jobs or land allocation settle the issue.
The figures 600 and 1,200 do not establish a benefit-cost result; no numerical comparison is warranted.
Condition missing: Whether industrial use actually restricts access or deprives residents of daily needs.

Whether industrial use actually restricts access or deprives residents of daily needs.

original_question.stem: A household is assigned a small agricultural plot for use, not ownership. In one period, the plot generates gross income of ₹1,20,000, and the household pays the stipulated tax of ₹18,000. There are no other deductions, and the household may keep all income remaining after this tax. Which entry correctly records the household’s land status and retained income?
options: The household owns the plot and retains ₹1,02,000.
The household may use, but does not own, the plot and retains ₹1,38,000.
The household may use, but does not own, the plot and retains ₹18,000.
The household may use, but does not own, the plot and retains ₹1,02,000.

items.original_explanation: The retained income is ₹1,20,000 − ₹18,000 = ₹1,02,000. The household has use, not ownership, of the plot, and may keep the income remaining after paying the stipulated tax. Therefore, the record should show use without ownership and ₹1,02,000 retained.

reasons: The source describes plots allocated for use, not ownership, and says households could keep land income after paying stipulated taxes (E1.1).
Retained income = ₹1,20,000 − ₹18,000 = ₹1,02,000, so D gives both the land status and the correct amount.

They reduced manufacturing efficiency and competitiveness, contributing to faster growth.
They reduced manufacturing efficiency but raised competitiveness, contributing to slower growth.

original_question.stem:
In each case, the initially announced fixed exchange rate is ₹80 per unit of foreign currency. The quote is expressed in rupees per unit of foreign currency, and the change is made by the government. Calculate the percentage change relative to ₹80 and match each case with its interpretation.

List-I
(A) The government raises the quote from ₹80 to ₹88.
(B) The government lowers the quote from ₹80 to ₹72.
(C) The government raises the quote from ₹80 to ₹84.
(D) The government lowers the quote from ₹80 to ₹76.

List-II
(I) Increase of 10%; devaluation; domestic currency becomes cheaper
(II) Decrease of 10%; revaluation; domestic currency becomes costlier
(III) Increase of 5%; devaluation; domestic currency becomes cheaper
(IV) Decrease of 5%; revaluation; domestic currency becomes costlier

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

items.original_explanation: The changes from ₹80 are ₹8 for (A) and (B), or 10%, and ₹4 for (C) and (D), or 5%. An increase in the exchange rate in a fixed system is devaluation, which makes the domestic currency cheaper; a decrease is revaluation, which makes it costlier. Therefore, the matching in option A is correct.

reasons: The supplied rule says a government increase in the exchange rate under a fixed system is devaluation (domestic currency cheaper); a decrease is revaluation (domestic currency costlier). Therefore the matching is A–I, B–II, C–III, D–IV (Option A).

On the other hand, a Revaluation is said to occur, when the Government decreases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency costlier) in a fixed exchange rate system.

86 86868686Introductory Macroeconomics economic agents will accept a national currency only if they are convinced that the amount of goods they can buy with a certain amount of that currency will not change frequently. In other words, the currency will maintain a stable purchasing power. Without this confidence, a currency will not be used as an international medium of exchange and unit of account since there is no international authority with the power to force the use of a particular currency in international transactions. In the past, governments have tried to gain confidence of potential users by announcing that the national currency will be freely convertible at a fixed price into another asset. Also, the issuing authority will have no control over the value of that asset into which the currency can be converted. This other asset most often has been gold, or other national currencies. There are two aspects of this commitment that has affected its credibility — the ability to convert freely in unlimited amounts and the price at which this conversion takes place. The international monetary system has been set up to handle these issues and ensure stability in international transactions. With the increase in the volume of transactions, gold ceased to be the asset into which national currencies could be converted (See Box 6.2). Although some national currencies have international acceptability, what is important in transactions between two countries is the currency in which the trade occurs. For instance, if an Indian wants to buy a good made in America, she would need dollars to complete the transaction. If the price of the good is ten dollars, she would need to know how much it would cost her in Indian rupees. That is, she will need to know the price of dollar in terms of rupees. The price of one currency in terms of another currency is known as the foreign exchange rate or simply the exchange rate . We will discuss this in detail in section 6.2. 6.1 THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year. There are two main accounts in the BoP — the current account and the capital account1. 6.1.1 Current Account Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments. Figure 6.1 illustrates the components of Current Account. Trade in goods includes exports and imports of goods. Trade in services includes factor income and non-factor income transactions. Transfer payments are the receipts which the residents of a country get for ‘free’, without having to provide any goods or services in return. They consist of gifts, remittances and grants. They could be given by the government or by private citizens living abroad. 1 There is a new classification in which the balance of payments have been divided into three accounts — the current account, the financial account and the capital account. This is as per the new accounting standards specified by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in the sixth edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6). India has also made the change but the Reserve Bank of India continues to publish data accounting to the old classification. Reprint 2026-27

original_question.stem: Only households and firms participate in an economy during a year. There is no saving, government, external trade or other leakage. Households spend all their income on final goods and services produced by domestic firms, and firms distribute their sales revenue as factor payments. An analyst records household spending received by Firm P as ₹3,25,000 and by Firm Q as ₹2,35,000. The value of final goods and services produced is ₹5,60,000, while recorded aggregate factor payments are ₹5,30,000. What adjustment must be made to the reported factor payments for the records to fit this model? Treat an increase as positive and a decrease as negative.

items.original_explanation: The two spending amounts total ₹5,60,000, matching the stated value of output. In this no-leakage two-sector model, aggregate consumption expenditure received as sales revenue equals factor payments. Factor payments must therefore increase from ₹5,30,000 to ₹5,60,000, an adjustment of ₹30,000.

reasons: Household spending totals ₹3,25,000 + ₹2,35,000 = ₹5,60,000, matching final output. In this no-leakage model, factor payments must also equal ₹5,60,000. The adjustment is ₹5,60,000 − ₹5,30,000 = +₹30,000.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Circular flow of income in a two-sector economy; expenditure, output and factor-income equality.

answer_conditions.condition: The economy has only households and firms, no leakages, and firms distribute their sales revenue as factor payments.
Household spending received by the firms totals ₹5,60,000 (₹3,25,000 + ₹2,35,000).
The value of final goods and services produced is ₹5,60,000.
Recorded aggregate factor payments are ₹5,30,000.
Under the stated no-leakage model, aggregate factor payments equal aggregate consumption expenditure and output value.
An increase is positive and a decrease is negative.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: Treat the matching ₹5,60,000 spending and output totals as the only records to reconcile, leaving the explicitly reported factor-payment total aside.
If the adjustment sums separate ₹30,000 corrections to both the factor-payment and expenditure records, the combined correction is ₹60,000.
Read the signed adjustment as recorded payments minus required payments: ₹5,30,000 − ₹5,60,000 = −₹30,000.

style_notes: The firm-specific spending totals and the stated output value provide a useful consistency check.

syllabus_objective.evidence: Tests the syllabus-named circular flow of income and equality of expenditure, output and factor income.

format_authenticity.evidence: A valid four-option numerical case application, with slightly more contextual detail than the matched direct-calculation exemplar.

level_calibration.evidence: Requires a standard model application and a simple calculation, comparable to the one-step GDP-deflator calculation.

discrimination_value.evidence: The options distinguish ignoring the gap, doubling it, reversing its sign, and applying the model correctly.

When the aggr egate revenue received by the firms is paid out to the factors of production it takes the form of aggregate income. In Fig. 2.1, the uppermost arrow, going from the households to the firms, represents the spending the households undertake to buy goods and services produced by the firms. The second arrow going from the firms to the households is the counterpart of the arrow above. It stands for the goods and services which are flowing from the firms to the households. In other words, this flow is what the households are getting from the firms, for which they are making the expenditures. In short, the two arrows on the top represent the goods and services market – the arrow above represents the flow of payments for the goods and services, the arrow below represents the flow of goods and services. The two arrows at the bottom of the diagram similarly represent the factors of production market. The lower most arrow going from the households to the firms symbolises the services that the households are rendering to the firms. Using these services the firms are manufacturing the output. The arrow above this, going from the firms to the households, represents the payments made by the firms to the households for the services provided by the latter. original_question.stem: A hypothetical trade arrangement requires developing countries to admit goods from developed countries, while developed countries do not admit goods from developing countries. Which feature of this arrangement matches the criticism that developing countries feel cheated?
options: Developed countries must open their markets to developing-country goods, while developing countries may exclude developed-country goods.
Developing countries must open their markets to developed-country goods, while developed countries exclude developing-country goods.
Both groups must open their markets to each other's goods.
Neither group must open its market, but developing-country goods are excluded from developed-country markets.

items.original_explanation: The criticism concerns unequal market access: developing countries are required to open their markets to developed-country goods but are not allowed access to developed-country markets. Option B matches both directions of the arrangement stated in the stem.

reasons: Option B matches the stated asymmetry: developing countries admit developed-country goods, while developed countries deny access to developing-country goods. The NCERT passage describes this as the criticism behind developing countries feeling cheated (E1.1, E1.2).
A reverses the arrangement; C makes access mutual; D removes the stated requirement on developing countries. No calculation is needed.

C would fit if both groups admitted each other's goods, rather than the one-way access stated in the stem.
D would fit if developing countries were not required to admit developed-country goods, while developed countries still denied market access.

original_question.stem:
A colonial official is reported as saying: “India is the pivot of our Empire... If the Empire loses any other part of its Dominion we can survive, but if we lose India, the sun of our Empire will have set.” The statement is attributed to Victor Alexander Vruce, Viceroy of British India in 1894. Match each part of the statement or its attribution in List-I with the interpretation it supports in List-II.

List-I

supporting_excerpts.text: 4 INDIAN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 1.1 I NTRODUCTION The primary objective of this book, Indian Economic Development , is to familiarise you with the basic features of the Indian economy, and its development, as it is today, in the aftermath of Independence. However, it is equally important to know something about the country’s economic past even as you learn about its present state and future prospects. So, let us first look at the state of India’s economy prior to the country’s independence and form an idea of the various considerations that shaped India’ s post-independence development strategy. The structure of India’s present- day economy is not just of current making; it has its roots steeped in history, particularly in the period when India was under British rule which lasted for almost two centuries before India finally won its independence on 15 August 1947. The sole purpose of the British colonial rule in India was to reduce the country to being a raw material supplier for Great Britain’s own rapidly expanding modern industrial base. An understanding of the exploitative nature of this relationship is essential for any assessment of the kind and level of development which the Indian economy has been able to attain over the last seven and half decades. 1.2 1.2 LOW LEVEL OF ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT UNDER THE COLONIAL RULE India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities. India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc. These products enjoyed a worldwide market based on the reputation of the fine quality of material used and the high standards of craftsmanship seen in all imports from India (See Box 1.1). “India is the pivot of our Empire... The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain.

A rural planning team is identifying water-body types relevant to a fishing community. The team is classifying types, not asserting that fishing takes place at each particular site. Consider the following statements.

original_question.stem: Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, the initial price of ₹1 is $0.0131. Which later quoted price of ₹1 indicates appreciation of the rupee compared with the initial price?

items.original_explanation: The price rises from $0.0131 to $0.0135 per ₹1. Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, an increase in the price of domestic currency (rupees) in foreign currency (dollars) is appreciation. The other listed prices are lower than or equal to the initial price.

reasons: E1.1 defines appreciation under a flexible exchange rate as an increase in the price of domestic currency in terms of foreign currency. Here $0.0135 is greater than $0.0131, so B indicates appreciation; $0.0131 is unchanged and the other quotes are lower.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Flexible exchange rates; appreciation of domestic currency quoted in terms of foreign currency.

answer_conditions.condition: The exchange-rate regime is flexible.
The initial price of ₹1 is $0.0131.

In a flexible exchange-rate regime, an increase in the domestic currency's price in foreign currency indicates appreciation.
Among the listed later prices, only $0.0135 is greater than $0.0131.

supporting_excerpts.text: Similarly, in a flexible exchange rate regime, when the price of domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars) increases, it is called Appreciation of the domestic currency (rupees) in terms of foreign currency (dollars).

Fixed Exchange Rates In this exchange rate system, the Government fixes the exchange rate at a particular level. In Fig. 6.3, the market determined exchange rate is e. However, let us suppose that for some reason the Indian Government wants to encourage exports for which it needs to make rupee cheaper for foreigners it would do so by fixing a higher exchange rate, say Rs 70 per dollar from the current exchange rate of Rs 50 per dollar. Thus, the new exchange rate set by the Government is e1, where e1 > e. At this exchange rate, the supply of dollars exceeds the demand for dollars. The RBI intervenes to purchase the dollars for rupees in the foreign exchange market in order to absorb this excess supply which has been marked as AB in the figure. Thus, through intervention, the Government can maintain any exchange rate in the economy. But it will be accumulating more and more foreign exchange so long as this intervention goes on. On the other hand if the goverment was to set an exchange rate at a level such as e 2, there would be an excess demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market. To meet this excess demand for dollars, the government would have to withdraw dollars from its past holdings of dollars. If it fails to do so, a black market for dollars may come up. In a fixed exchange rate system, when some government action increases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency cheaper) is called Devaluation. On the other hand, a Revaluation is said to occur, when the Government decreases the exchange rate (thereby, making domestic currency costlier) in a fixed exchange rate system.

original_question.stem: A district planning panel reports that private schools and clinics are operating alongside public intervention in both sectors. Education and health-care services in the district create both private and social benefits, but many households cannot afford basic access to either service. Expenditure on both services has substantial long-term effects that are not easily reversed. Which recommendation is best supported for the district?
options: Withdraw public intervention in both sectors despite the affordability constraint.
Continue public intervention only in education because health care creates no social benefits.

Continue public intervention in both sectors because the services create private and social benefits, many households cannot afford access, and expenditure effects are substantial and not easily reversed.
Withdraw public intervention in both sectors because the expenditure effects are readily reversible.

items.original_explanation: Both services create private and social benefits, many households cannot afford basic access, and expenditure on these services has substantial long-term effects that are not easily reversed. These stated conditions support public intervention in both sectors, which is already operating in the district.

reasons: The stem supplies the relevant district facts: both sectors have private and public provision, the services create private and social benefits, many households cannot afford access, and the effects are long-term and hard to reverse.

The excerpts link private and social benefits to the coexistence of public and private institutions, and conclude that government intervention is essential in light of affordability constraints and the lasting effects of education and health expenditure. Option C applies that rationale to both sectors.
